A big toe that hurts with every step
is not something you have to put up with.

If the skin beside the nail is red and swollen and throbs as soon as you put shoes on, it may be an ingrown toenail.
In the early stages it can improve without removing the nail.

intro:
What an ingrown toenail actually is

The side corner at the end of the nail digs into the flesh beside it, and that spot becomes inflamed and painful.

It helps to picture a small splinter lodged in the skin, pricking continuously. A splinter can simply be pulled out, but a nail keeps growing, so if it is left alone it digs in deeper. In medical terms it is also called onychocryptosis. All the names describe the same condition.

It occurs mostly on the big toe, because that is the toe that carries the most body weight when you walk and is pressed hardest by footwear. It is common in teenagers, but it can happen to anyone at any age.

Could this be me? A self-check

If even one of these applies, it may be an ingrown toenail
  • the skin beside the big toenail is red and swollen
  • it throbs beside the nail when you put shoes on or walk
  • pressing the area hurts and feels hot
  • clear fluid or pus is visible
  • a red lump of tissue is rising beside the nail (medically, granulation tissue)
  • there is an odour, and the pain makes walking difficult
  • just as it seems to settle, the same spot hurts again

How it progresses

  1. Stage 1The side of the nail reddens and swells a little. Mildly painful.
  2. Stage 2Under more pressure the swelling grows and fluid begins to seep.
  3. Stage 3A red lump of tissue grows up out of the groove.
  4. Stage 4It suppurates and smells, and the pain makes walking hard.

Why has this happened to me?

The cause comes down to one thing. A situation has been created in which the nail presses continuously on the flesh beside it.

  • Cutting nails short and rounded — the most common cause. Scooping the corners into a curve lets the flesh cover the gap, and the nail then grows back out into that flesh and pricks it.
  • Tight footwear — narrow shoes, pointed toes and high heels worn for long periods keep pressing the nail into the flesh. It is especially common in people who stand all day or spend long hours walking in dress shoes.
  • A nail thickened by fungal infection — a thickened nail digs into flesh far more easily. Without treating the fungal infection at the same time, it keeps recurring.
  • A protruding or differently shaped toe bone — pressure can concentrate on one side.
  • Age, weight and family history — nails curl inward with age, and added weight increases the pressure on the toes.
  • Diabetes, or feet that sweat a great deal — wounds form easily and heal poorly, so the risk is greater.

If you leave it, thinking it will settle in a few days

An ingrown toenail is not a condition that can be waited out. Because the nail keeps growing, the situation generally worsens unless the cause is removed.

  • Pain interferes with walking, exercise and daily life.
  • If the inflammation worsens, it can spread into a bacterial infection with swelling and fever across the whole toe (cellulitis).
  • Once the red lump of tissue grows, treatment becomes more complex and recovery takes longer.
If you have diabetes — please do not try to deal with it yourself

Diabetes reduces circulation and sensation in the feet. Small foot wounds therefore heal poorly and can develop into serious infection. If you have diabetes, take particular care with nail care, and it is safer to be seen by a doctor before touching it at home.

Treatment options

In most cases the diagnosis is made by looking at the toe directly, with no special tests. If a fungal nail infection is also suspected, a fungal test may be added.

Treatment depends on how severe it is and how many times it has recurred. What matters is that in the early stages it can improve without removing the nail. The sooner you come while it hurts, the more options you have.

MethodWhen it is usedWhat it involves
① Conservative careEarly, with mild inflammationSterile cotton or dental floss is placed between the ingrown corner and the flesh to separate them. This alone can resolve it without surgery in some cases
② MedicationWhen there is pus or bacterial infectionAntibiotics settle the inflammation first, and the next step is decided afterwards
③ Corrective deviceWhen the nail is curledThe spring of a clip or wire gradually flattens the curled nail. No nail is removed
④ SurgeryWhen inflammation is severe or it keeps recurringUnder local anaesthesia of the toe alone, the ingrown portion is removed and the nail root treated so that it does not grow into the same place again

※ The type of corrective device, where it can be used and how long treatment takes all depend on the state of the nail. We explain this in detail at your consultation. Where part of the nail root is treated during surgery, the nail stays narrower in that area; this is part of preventing recurrence.

How to cut your nails to prevent recurrence

Treatment alone is not enough. If the habits that caused it remain, it comes back. Treatment and prevention must go together.

Nail care

  • Cut toenails straight across. Do not scoop the corners into a curve.
  • Leave both corners so that their tips are always visible outside the flesh.
  • Do not push the clippers deep down the sides of the nail.
  • Do not cut too short; keep a reasonable length.

Footwear and daily life

  • Avoid tight shoes, pointed toes and high heels; wear shoes that fit.
  • Wash your feet and dry them thoroughly.
  • Reduce activities that strain the feet and rest enough. Keep to a healthy weight.
  • If you have diabetes, inspect your feet visually every day.
Please do not do these
  • cutting the nail even shorter because it hurts — it digs in further
  • picking or digging at the nail or toe with fingers or tools
  • continuing to wear tight shoes

Come in without delay if

  • home care has not improved it
  • the toe is badly swollen and painful and pus is coming out
  • you have a fever or chills
  • you have diabetes — be seen before touching it at home
  • it keeps coming back in the same place
outro:
Frequently asked questions

Does the nail have to be removed?
No. Early on, with mild inflammation, placing sterile cotton or dental floss between the ingrown corner and the flesh can be enough. However, where it has already suppurated badly or keeps recurring, surgery may be needed. It depends on your condition, so an examination gives the most accurate answer.
Does it hurt a lot? What kind of anaesthesia?
Surgery is carried out under local anaesthesia of the toe only. General anaesthesia is not used. How long it takes and how long recovery lasts depend on your condition, and we explain this at your consultation.
Will the nail grow back oddly after treatment?
Where part of the nail root is treated during surgery, the nail stays narrower in that area. This is part of preventing the nail from digging into the same place again. How much narrower depends on how far it had grown in, so we explain this in advance at your consultation.
Why does it keep coming back?
Because the habits and conditions that caused it are still there. Cutting nails straight across, avoiding tight shoes, keeping feet clean and dry and maintaining a healthy weight must be kept up alongside treatment.
I also have a fungal nail infection — does it matter?
It matters a great deal. When a fungal infection thickens and distorts the nail, it digs into flesh far more easily. In that case both conditions must be treated together to reduce recurrence, and a fungal test is performed where necessary.
Which toe is most often affected?
The big toe, and most often on the right foot, because that is where walking pressure is greatest.

Please note

The content of this page is general medical information and does not replace diagnosis and treatment of an individual patient. Symptoms, treatment methods and outcomes vary with each patient's condition. Please decide on an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan through consultation with our medical team.
